tagline: A parkway reshaped by wetlands, with a trail beside the traffic.
intro: Legacy Parkway curves along Great Salt Lake wetlands, with nature preserves to the west and rail lines and I-15 to the east. Visit Utah highlights lake views and the millions of migrating birds that feed here each spring and fall. Utah designated the parkway a state scenic byway in 2002; in 2018, the designation was renamed Great Salt Lake Scenic Byway and extended toward Antelope Island Marina.

Construction started in 2001, then stopped amid lawsuits over the environmental review. A federal appeals court found the review inadequate for failing to study alternative routes less harmful to wetlands. A revised review changed the alignment and enlarged Legacy Nature Preserve; Utah and the Sierra Club signed a compromise in 2005. The road opened in September 2008 as a four-lane parkway instead of the planned six-lane expressway. The settlement initially limited speeds and excluded semi-trucks except in specified circumstances. Those restrictions expired on January 1, 2020, when trucks were allowed and the speed limit rose to 65 mph.

Heading south, begin at Farmington’s Wasatch Weave interchange west of Lagoon. Continue past Centerville and West Bountiful’s wetland curves, then through Woods Cross toward I-215. Legacy Nature Preserve borders the southern stretch, and the Legacy Parkway Trail parallels the entire road.
notice: The road follows the wetland contours at West Bountiful.

moments.title: Farmington
moments.text: Farmington’s Lagoon began with a resort that lost its lakeshore. The Denver & Rio Grande Western Railroad built Lake Park on Great Salt Lake in 1886, but retreating water left it stranded inland. After it closed in 1895, Simon Bamberger bought most of its buildings and moved them about three miles east to attract passengers to his Salt Lake & Ogden Railroad. Lagoon opened at Farmington in July 1896. Its name came from the small body of water on the original forty-acre property. The park added a wooden roller coaster in 1921, designed by John Miller, as rides joined the original music and restaurants.

moments.title: Centerville
moments.text: Centerville occupies a narrow strip between the Wasatch Mountains and Farmington Bay. Its name began as a measurement: an 1850 survey placed the town precisely between Farmington and Bountiful. Before that, it had been Deuel Settlement and then Cherry Creek, named after the Cherry family. Shadrach Roundy built a gristmill on Deuel Creek in the winter of 1849 and also used it to make molasses from corn stalks. The Utah Central Rail Road reached Centerville in 1869. The settlement preceded the name: Thomas Grover arrived in the autumn of 1847, and a log schoolhouse followed in 1851.

moments.title: Legacy Nature Preserve
moments.text: Near the parkway’s southern end, the road forms Legacy Nature Preserve’s eastern boundary. The preserve gained land when a supplemental environmental review changed the highway’s route in 2005. That review also added the trail system beside the road. The redesign protected wetlands west of the pavement and in the median, with pedestrian bridges and underpasses connecting the trail system. Along the full parkway, protected land totals 2,225 acres to the west, with another 20 acres of wetlands along the highway. Farther north, the road also forms much of the eastern edge of Farmington Bay Waterfowl Management Area.
